name: Vienna Gate
description: A rebuilt gateway at the northern end of the Castle District, where several well-known streets meet. The present gate dates from 1936, marking 250 years since the recapture of Buda, and replaced older gates that stood here since the Middle Ages.

children.text: The Vienna Gate, Bécsi kapu in Hungarian, stands at the northeastern corner of Vienna Gate Square at the northern end of the Castle District. It is the gate that linked the Castle to the road to Vienna. Visit Buda Castle calls it one of the most atmospheric entrances to Buda Castle and notes that several well-known Castle District streets begin at the square. Nearby it lists the Hungarian National Archives, the Lutheran church of Buda Castle and a notable grapevine.

A gate has stood here since the Middle Ages, and the names show its past. In the Middle Ages it was the Porta Sabbati, or Szombat-kapu, the Saturday Gate, after the weekly markets held in front of it. In the Ottoman period it was called Beç kapusu, and it was later also known as the Zsidó-kapu, the Jewish Gate. The Castle District heritage site says the medieval layout is known only from Baroque and late Ottoman plans, which show a tower where the wall sections met, with the passage through its ground floor.

The gate was rebuilt several times. A new one was built in 1723 and remained in use until 1849; another followed in 1850. In the early nineteenth century one of its two side gates was removed, and before the 1896 millenary festival the whole gate was pulled down. The present gate was built in 1936 to mark the 250th anniversary of the recapture of Buda from the Ottomans, and it resembles the destroyed one.

Wikipedia names the architect as Jenő Kismarty-Lechner and says the sculptor Béla Ohmann made the inscriptions, ornaments and reliefs, including a running angel. Memorials to the 1686 recapture stand on both sides: an angel statue on the left and a tablet on the right. Wikipedia describes the gate as more symbolic than functional. Two parts of the Bastion Promenade are connected across its top, and automatic barriers at the gate help control traffic within the Castle.
Good to know
Walk through the gate to see the angel statue and the tablet commemorating the 1686 recapture on either side.
The Lutheran church of Buda Castle and the Hungarian National Archives are close by on the square.
Several of the best-known Castle District streets start at the square, so it works well as an entry point for a walk through the district.

children.text: A gate stood here in the Middle Ages, connecting the Castle with the road to Vienna. It was called the Szombat-kapu, the Saturday Gate, because markets were held in front of it every Saturday. The Ottomans called it Beç kapusu, and it later became known as the Zsidó-kapu, the Jewish Gate.

One of its two side gates was removed in the early nineteenth century and the whole gate was demolished in 1896. The present gate was rebuilt in 1936, commemorating the 250th anniversary of the recapture of Buda, and was designed by Jenő Kismarty-Lechner, with inscriptions, ornaments and reliefs, including a running angel, by the sculptor Béla Ohmann. Its value is symbolic rather than defensive, although automatic barriers at the gate now help to limit traffic in the Castle, and two parts of the Bastion Promenade are connected across its top.

name: The Tabán
description: A green slope between Buda Castle, Gellért Hill and Naphegy, on the site of the old Tabán quarter of winding streets, taverns and Serbian, Greek and German residents. The district was largely demolished in the 1930s, and today a quiet park near Döbrentei Square marks its place.

children.text: The Tabán is a park in Buda's 1st district between Buda Castle, Gellért Hill and Naphegy, near Döbrentei Square. The Visit Buda Castle page calls it a quiet place for a walk, a picnic or a pause while sightseeing, and says it occupies the site of a quarter of winding streets, restaurants and wine taverns that many called the Montmartre of Budapest.

The area has long been settled thanks to its sheltered valley, the thermal waters at the foot of Gellért Hill and a ford across the Danube. After the 1686 liberation of Buda, refugees arrived from Greece, Bosnia and Serbia, and Wikipedia says that in the 18th century the residents included Serbs, Greeks, Vlachs, Germans, Croats, Slovaks and Romani people. The Serbs were called Rácok, which gave the district the name Rácváros.

In the early 20th century its houses were considered unhealthy, and the Tabán was demolished in the 1930s because of overcrowding and poor public health. Hungarian Wikipedia says the planned new district was never built because of the Second World War, and that the area was landscaped as a public park in the 1960s. Wikipedia also records the 1956 memorial near Naphegy and Kereszt streets and the Semmelweis Museum of Medical History near Apród Street. The Rác Thermal Bath near Döbrentei Square was listed as closed on the Visit Buda Castle page, so check its current status.
Good to know
The park is near Döbrentei Square, at the foot of the Tabán, and lies between Buda Castle and Gellért Hill, so it suits a walk between the two.
The Rác Thermal Bath is nearby but has been closed for refurbishment for many years, and its reopening is still only a plan, so check the operator before counting on it.
The Semmelweis Museum of Medical History is near Apród Street, and the 1956 memorial is near Naphegy and Kereszt streets.

historyIntro: The Tabán was a quarter of Buda that stood for centuries on the river side of Castle Hill and was largely demolished in the 1930s. The park there today replaced it.

children.text: Wikipedia says the area has been inhabited since Neolithic times thanks to a sheltered valley, thermal waters at the foot of Gellért Hill and a ford over the Danube, and that the Romans replaced the Celts in the 1st century BC. In the Middle Ages the Tabán lay outside the walls and became a suburb of Buda, according to Hungarian Wikipedia. The Turks developed thermal medicinal baths there and brought in settlers from the Balkans. After the 1686 liberation of Buda refugees arrived from Greece, Bosnia and Serbia, and the Habsburg authorities resettled roughly 600 Serbian families in the Lower Town; a 1696 census recorded more than 1,000 Serbian families. The district was also known as Raitzenstadt, the town of the Serbs.

Franciscans from Bosnia founded the parish Church of St Catherine of Alexandria in the 17th century, and it was rebuilt in Baroque style between 1728 and 1777. The Serbian community's Church of St Demetrius was built in Baroque style from 1742, consecrated in 1751 and given a copper spire in 1775. The Great Tabán Fire of 1810 burned out the church, and the 1838 flood damaged it again. By the 19th century the Tabán was a bohemian quarter with many restaurants, bars and brothels, its narrow hillside streets giving it a Mediterranean feel, and Kereszt Street was its centre.

Because of overcrowding and poor public health, the Tabán was demolished in the 1930s: The English Wikipedia article on the Church of St Demetrius dates the main clearance to 1933 to 1934 and the last surrounding buildings to 1938, while Hungarian Wikipedia says the houses were demolished between 1933 and 1936. Hungarian Wikipedia says the planned new district was never built because of the Second World War, and that the area was landscaped as a public park in the 1960s. The Church of St Demetrius survived the clearance but was seriously damaged in the siege of 1944 and 1945 and the ruin was demolished in 1949. The Tabán school was destroyed in January 1945. Today the Tabán is a park, with the Semmelweis Museum of Medical History and a 1956 memorial nearby.

name: Matthias Fountain
description: A neo-Baroque bronze fountain group by Alajos Stróbl in the Buda Castle palace forecourt, showing King Matthias Corvinus on a hunt. It was inaugurated in 1904, damaged in the Second World War, and is sometimes nicknamed the Trevi Fountain of Budapest.

children.text: The Matthias Fountain, Mátyás kútja, is a monumental fountain group in the western forecourt of Buda Castle, set against the northern facade of the former Castle Church. Visit Buda Castle places it in the Hunyadi Courtyard of the palace and describes it as Alajos Stróbl's sculptural composition evoking the legend of the Renaissance ruler, with cascading water. English Wikipedia calls the style neo-Baroque and says it is sometimes called the Trevi Fountain of Budapest.

The scene is a hunting party led by King Matthias Corvinus. The king stands on the highest rock in hunting dress with a crossbow in his right hand and a huge dead stag at his feet. Below him a henchman blows a horn, the leader of the hunting group sits on a boulder with his back to the viewer, and three hounds complete the central group. The bronze figures stand on heaps of rocks, with water running down between the boulders. The central niche forms a triumphal arch bearing the king's personal coat of arms.

Two figures sit at the sides of the basin. On the right is Szép Ilonka, Helen the Fair, protecting her tame fawn from the hunters. She is the heroine of a nineteenth-century ballad by Mihály Vörösmarty. On the left is Galeotto Marzio, an Italian chronicler who lived at Matthias's court, with a sighthound at his feet and a falcon on his fist.

Stróbl began work in 1899 after King Franz Joseph approved the composition. According to Wikipedia, the stag was modelled on a large animal killed by poachers in 1896 in a forest where Stróbl had gone hunting, and Duke Pálffy sent the hounds that served as models. The henchman figure won a state gold medal in 1901. The fountain was inaugurated in 1904 in the king's presence, and Alajos Hauszmann, master builder of the palace reconstruction, is credited with erecting it.

The Second World War destroyed the middle dog, which Jenő Grantner later reconstructed. The more elaborate original balustrade and mansard roof were simplified after the war damage, and the fountain was restored in 2010.
Good to know
Look for the details at the basin: Szép Ilonka and her fawn on the right, Galeotto Marzio with his falcon on the left.
The fountain is part of the palace grounds; check the official Buda Castle pages for current access to the courtyards.
The Savoyai Terrace and the Hungarian National Gallery are also in the palace area, so the two sights combine easily.

heroImage.alt: The bronze Matthias Fountain depicting a royal hunting scene in the Buda Castle courtyard

historyIntro: The Matthias Fountain was made by Alajos Stróbl between 1899 and 1904 as part of the great reconstruction of the Buda palace. It lost a figure in the Second World War and was restored in 2010.

historySections.heading: The palace that needed a fountain, 1875 to 1912

children.text: English Wikipedia's history of Buda Castle says the rebuilding of the palace spanned 1875 to 1912. Miklós Ybl drew a master plan in 1885 and work began in 1890, and after his death in 1891 Alajos Hauszmann took over. Hauszmann designed the north wing, which doubled the Baroque palace on the Danube side. The same history places Alajos Stróbl's fountain in the western forecourt near the rear facade of that wing, as part of Hauszmann's work. The fountain's own article credits Hauszmann as master builder of the palace reconstruction and as the man who erected the fountain.

According to English Wikipedia, King Franz Joseph approved the scheme, and Stróbl began work in 1899. He modelled the stag on a large animal killed by poachers in 1896 in a forest where he had gone hunting, and Duke Pálffy sent him the hounds that served as models. The figure of the henchman won a state gold medal in 1901. The fountain was inaugurated in 1904 in the presence of the king. It shows King Matthias Corvinus in hunting dress above a dead stag, with Szép Ilonka and the chronicler Galeotto Marzio at the sides of the basin.

The group suffered in the Second World War, when the middle dog sculpture was destroyed. The sculptor Jenő Grantner reconstructed it. Wikipedia adds that the original balustrade and mansard roof, which had been more elaborate, were simplified after the war damage. This matches the wider history of the palace, which was reduced to ruins in the siege of 1944 and 1945 and rebuilt in the following decades. The fountain was restored in 2010, and it stands today in the palace forecourt that Visit Buda Castle calls the Hunyadi Courtyard.

One of the figures at the basin is Szép Ilonka, Helen the Fair, shown protecting her tame fawn. She is the heroine of a nineteenth-century ballad by Mihály Vörösmarty. According to the ballad, Ilonka and Matthias fell in love when he was hunting without revealing who he was; when she learned his true identity she assumed the love was impossible and died of a broken heart. This is a literary legend, not a documented event.

name: Savoyai Terrace
description: A broad terrace in front of the Hungarian National Gallery on the Danube side of Buda Castle, with views of the Parliament, Gellért Hill and the bridges. Its centrepiece is József Róna's equestrian statue of Prince Eugene of Savoy, installed in 1900.

children.text: The Savoyai Terrace lies in front of the Hungarian National Gallery on the Danube side of the Buda palace. Visit Buda Castle says it offers a stunning view of the Danube, the Parliament, Gellért Hill and the bridges of Budapest, and that it features an equestrian statue of Eugene of Savoy. Wikipedia lists the Hungarian National Gallery, founded in 1957, among the palace wings labelled A to D.

The terrace is named after Prince Eugene of Savoy, born in Paris on 18 October 1663 and died in Vienna on 21 April 1736. According to Hungary Today he served as deputy commander of the Christian forces that liberated Buda in 1686. On 11 September 1697 he defeated a numerically superior Ottoman army at the Battle of Zenta, which the same article says ended roughly 150 years of Ottoman rule in Hungary.

The statue is the work of the sculptor József Róna. One account says the city of Zenta ordered it to commemorate the victory of 1697 but could not pay for the bronze, so it waited in Róna's studio and then in front of the Art Gallery's main entrance. Prime Minister Kálmán Széll suggested that Emperor Franz Joseph buy it, and he did, judging by photographs. It was installed in 1900 in front of the main facade of the Royal Palace. That account describes its style as Viennese neo-Baroque, chosen to harmonise with the horseshoe-shaped Baroque staircase behind it.

The palace around the terrace changed greatly in the twentieth century. English Wikipedia says fighting in the siege of 1944 and 1945 reduced the palace to ruins. The Baroque staircase was demolished in the 1950s and not restored, but the statue survived the siege relatively intact and returned to its original place after restoration.
Good to know
Come for the view: the terrace looks across the Danube towards the Parliament, with Gellért Hill and several bridges in sight.
The Matthias Fountain and the Hungarian National Gallery are in the same palace area, so the three sights fit into one visit.
Check the official Buda Castle and Hungarian National Gallery pages for current access conditions and events on the terrace.

historyIntro: The terrace takes its name from Prince Eugene of Savoy, whose equestrian statue by József Róna was placed before the Buda palace in 1900. The statue was first made for the town of Zenta and was bought for the palace instead.

children.text: Prince Eugene of Savoy was born in Paris on 18 October 1663 and died in Vienna on 21 April 1736. According to Hungary Today, he served as deputy commander of the Christian forces that liberated Buda in 1686. On 11 September 1697 he defeated a numerically superior Ottoman army at the Battle of Zenta, a victory the same article credits with ending roughly 150 years of Ottoman rule in Hungary. He also owned the island of Csepel, where he built a castle at Ráckeve, and Promontor, today's Budafok, was part of his estate.

The equestrian statue is the work of József Róna. One account says the city of Zenta ordered it to commemorate the victory of 1697 but could not pay for the bronze, which waited in the sculptor's studio and then in front of the Art Gallery's main entrance. Prime Minister Kálmán Széll suggested that Emperor Franz Joseph buy it, and he did so on the basis of photographs. The statue was installed in 1900 in front of the main facade of the Royal Palace in Buda. A list of equestrian statues in Hungary also gives it as by József Róna, in the Buda Castle, 1900.

historySections.heading: Siege, ruin and return, 1944 to the 1950s

children.text: The palace around the statue changed greatly after the siege of Budapest. English Wikipedia says that fighting between 29 December 1944 and 13 February 1945 reduced the palace to ruins. The Baroque horseshoe staircase behind the statue was demolished in the 1950s and not restored. The statue itself came through the siege relatively intact and, after restoration, returned to its original place. Today the terrace in front of the Hungarian National Gallery, with the statue at its centre, looks out over the Danube towards the Parliament, Gellért Hill and the city's bridges.
